candidate.blueprint_topic: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — IV insulin in severe diabetic ketoacidosis
candidate.educational_objective: Recognize continuous IV insulin as the recommended approach for severe DKA while understanding that selected uncomplicated mild or moderate DKA can be managed with subcutaneous rapid-acting insulin under an appropriate protocol.

options.A: Continuous IV insulin is appropriate for severe DKA, with protocol-based monitoring and adjustment as ketoacidosis resolves.
options.B: All DKA, including uncomplicated mild DKA, must be treated with continuous IV insulin in an intensive care setting.
options.C: IV insulin eliminates the need to monitor potassium because insulin does not affect serum potassium during DKA treatment.
options.D: Regular human insulin is the only insulin formulation that can ever be administered intravenously, which is why it must be used for every DKA case.

candidate.rationale: A is correct. The 2026 ADA Standards of Care state that severe DKA is managed with continuous intravenous insulin infusion using a fixed-rate or validated nurse-driven protocol. The 2024 international hyperglycemic-crisis consensus similarly identifies continuous IV short-acting insulin as the preferred approach for severe or complicated DKA, while uncomplicated mild or moderate DKA may be treated with subcutaneous rapid-acting insulin analogs in appropriate settings. C is unsafe because IV regular insulin labeling requires close glucose and potassium monitoring due to risks including hypoglycemia and hypokalemia. D is false: the rationale for IV treatment in severe DKA is clinical severity and titratable continuous insulin delivery, not a claim that regular insulin is the only insulin product approved for IV use.
candidate.source_claim_supported: Severe DKA is appropriately treated with continuous IV insulin using a validated protocol; selected uncomplicated mild/moderate DKA can be treated subcutaneously; IV regular insulin requires close glucose and potassium monitoring.
